response: Waiting half an hour without knowing why is hard, and it makes sense that you felt unimportant. It's worth knowing that a train cancellation stopped B from taking the planned train. That means the delay came from something outside B's control, not from B not caring about the dinner. You also noticed B seemed annoyed when they arrived. We only have your side, so we don't know what B was feeling. They may have been stressed from the journey. You could tell B how the wait felt for you and ask what their evening was like. That might clear things up for both of you.

It sounds stressful to be stuck on the platform, worried and wanting to get to dinner, and then to arrive to silence. The train cancellation was out of your control, and you tried to send a message. We don't know yet how A experienced the wait. They may not have received your message and may have felt worried or hurt sitting alone. Once things are calmer, it could help to share what happened on your end and to ask A how the evening felt for them. Then you could agree together on what to do if one of you is running late again.

It sounds like you both had a hard evening, each with only part of the picture. A, waiting without any news, it makes sense that you felt unimportant. B, you were stuck on a platform after a cancellation, anxious and trying to reach A, and you can't be sure your message arrived. The lateness came from the train, not from a lack of care. The tension when you met may have been two stressed people misreading each other. It could help to tell each other what those 30 minutes were like for you. Then you could agree on a backup way to get in touch when plans go wrong.

It sounds like you both had a hard evening, each without the full picture. B, you were anxious on the platform and trying to get there after the train was cancelled. A, you were waiting without any news, and it's understandable that you felt unimportant. The message may not have arrived, so A didn't know what had happened. B's lateness came from the cancellation, not from a lack of care. A, you read B as annoyed, and B, you found A unwilling to talk. Each of you could share what you were feeling in those moments. You could also agree on a backup way to reach each other when plans fall apart.

It sounds painful to come home and have B go off alone for twenty minutes. Feeling rejected in that moment makes sense. Still, what you've described is your reading of B's mood. B's own reasons haven't been heard yet, and time alone can mean many things, like decompressing after a long day. You two also have no explicit agreement about greetings. A calm conversation could help. You might tell B how that moment felt to you, ask what B needed, and agree together on a way of reconnecting that works for both of you.

B, it sounds like the noise at work left you depleted, and taking twenty minutes to decompress was a way to come back able to be present for A. That makes sense. Since you two never agreed on how greetings go, A may not know what that time alone means. I only have your side, so I can't say how A experienced it. A quick, warm word before you step away could help, something like "I'm fried, I need a few minutes, then I'm all yours." It might also be worth talking together about what each of you needs when you get home.

A, it makes sense that B disappearing into another room felt like rejection, and that hurt is real. B, your need for quiet after a noisy day makes sense too. You say you took the time so you could be present for A afterward. What's missing is a shared understanding. A read the silence as anger, but B describes overload, not anger. It might help to agree on a small signal, like "I need twenty minutes to decompress, then I'm all yours." That way the break doesn't feel like distance. A, it may also help to ask rather than assume "as usual."

Each of your accounts makes sense from where you stand. A, feeling rejected when B walked away is real and worth saying. B, needing quiet after a loud day is real too. B describes the break as a way to recover so they could be present for A afterward. That's different from anger, though only B can say what B felt. Neither of you had agreed on how homecomings should go, so it may help to set one up. For example, a quick hug and a 'I need twenty minutes, then I'm all yours' could let B rest without A feeling shut out.

It makes sense that finding the dishes still there felt like being taken for granted, especially since you two had agreed B would wash them. Your feeling is real. Still, you've said you haven't asked B what happened, so the reason isn't known yet. It could have been forgetting, being tired, something unexpected, or something else entirely. You might try something like: "I noticed the dishes were still in the sink this morning, and I felt taken for granted. What happened?" That names how you felt without assuming why B left them. It also gives you both a chance to talk about how to handle it next time.

B, it makes sense that an important, draining call pushed the dishes out of your mind. Forgetting after something like that is human, and your annoyance is understandable too. It may help to hold two things at once: the call mattered, and you had agreed to the dishes. A may feel let down even while understanding the call. Try leading with a simple acknowledgment, like "I said I'd do them and I didn't, sorry," before explaining the call. You could also suggest a backup, such as a reminder or a quick text when plans shift. Then A can understand without feeling the agreement didn't count.

It sounds like a small miss turned into two different stories. A, it makes sense that you felt taken for granted, but you've said you didn't ask what happened. B, you say you forgot after an important call. That explains the miss, but it doesn't erase the agreement. You might start with a simple acknowledgment: "I said I'd do them and didn't, sorry." Then you could explain the call. A could also try asking before reaching a conclusion. It may help for both of you to agree on what to do when plans slip, like sending a quick heads-up or doing the task first thing the next morning.

It sounds like this left both of you feeling unseen. B, you agreed to do the dishes, and a long, important call pushed them out of your mind. That makes sense. Saying so plainly and acknowledging the missed commitment will likely land better than asking A to understand. A, feeling taken for granted is real. But you guessed that B expected you to do them, and you didn't check. B says it was forgetting, not expectation. A short conversation could help: what happened, how it felt, and maybe a simple plan, such as a quick heads-up when plans get derailed.

It makes sense that you felt disappointed. You'd been picturing Saturday as time together, and that turned out not to be the plan. It's also true that the two of you hadn't actually agreed on it, so B may not have known you were expecting it. Whether B made plans to avoid you is something only B can say. Asking directly, without accusing, might help. You could also tell B that shared weekend time matters to you and suggest setting some aside ahead of time. That way your expectations are spoken out loud, and you're less likely to end up disappointed by plans neither of you made.

B, the shared facts back you up on the main point. You each made separate plans for Saturday afternoon, and you hadn't agreed to spend it together, so it makes sense that the disagreement surprised you. Calling A 'always so sensitive' may not help, though. We only have your side, and A may have had expectations or feelings that never got said out loud. It could help to ask A what Saturday meant to them, and to talk about how you'll check in about weekend time from now on. That way, neither of you is caught off guard again.

It sounds like you two had different expectations about Saturday, and you never talked them through. A, your disappointment makes sense if you were counting on time together. Still, nothing here shows that B was trying to avoid you. B, your surprise is understandable, since nothing had been agreed. Calling A 'always so sensitive' will likely shut the conversation down rather than help it. You might try saying out loud what you each expect from weekends and agreeing on how you'll plan shared time. That way, assumptions don't have to do the work that a quick conversation could.

It sounds like you went into Saturday with different expectations. You never agreed to spend it together, so A assumed it was shared time while B assumed you'd each do your own thing. A's disappointment and B's surprise both make sense given those different starting points. Some of the harder conclusions, like B wanting to avoid A, or A always being 'so sensitive,' go beyond what's known and could make things worse. It might help to talk about what weekend time means to each of you, and to agree more clearly on future plans so neither of you is left guessing.

Going four hours without a reply, and not being able to tell whether your message was even read, could easily leave you worried and wondering whether B was upset. Your worry makes sense. Still, what you've described doesn't show why B didn't answer. It doesn't show whether they saw the message, what they were doing, or how they were feeling. A calm check-in might help, something like: "I didn't hear back earlier and caught myself worrying. Is everything okay?" That shares how you felt without assuming a reason, and it gives B room to explain.

B, it sounds like you were trying to balance two real needs. You wanted to give your work your full attention, and you also didn't want A to feel ignored. Having your phone in your bag explains how four hours could pass without a reply. We don't know how that silence felt for A, though, because A's side isn't included here. It could help to ask A what they experienced and talk through a simple plan together, such as a quick note before you go heads-down or a set time when you'll check messages. That way you can focus without the gap feeling like distance.

It sounds like those four hours felt very different from each side. A, waiting without knowing whether the message had been read is hard, and it makes sense that you started wondering whether B was upset. B, you were heads-down at work with your phone in your bag, and you didn't want A to feel ignored. Neither of you seems to have done anything wrong. It might help to agree on a small habit, like a quick 'busy, will reply later' note or a heads-up before long focus stretches. That way silence is less likely to be read as a signal.

From both accounts, it sounds like two reasonable needs ran into each other. B needed uninterrupted time to work, with the phone tucked away. A was left with four hours of silence and no way to know whether the message had even been seen. That gap easily turns into worry about whether something is wrong. Neither account suggests bad intent. A small agreement might help. B could send a quick "heads down until 4" note before focusing, or a brief reply once free. A could check in about expectations instead of guessing. Talking through what each of you needs during work hours could keep this from happening again.

It makes sense that you felt upset when B questioned the purchase, especially since you saw it as useful for both of you. You're also being honest that you knew the two of you had agreed to discuss purchases over 100 units first, and this one was 120. Both things can be true: the item may well be useful, and skipping the agreed conversation may have mattered to B. It could help to acknowledge the missed step without getting defensive. Then talk through why you think the item is worthwhile. You could also ask B how they experienced it, since their view isn't included here.

B, it makes sense that you felt excluded. You both agreed to talk about purchases over 100 units, and this 120-unit purchase happened without that conversation. That's a real breach of the agreement. When you raise it with A, it may help to stick to this specific event: what was agreed, what happened, and how it felt for you. Words like 'always' and 'impulsive' can make A defensive. If this keeps happening, you could bring up a few concrete examples. You might also talk together about how to make the agreement easier to keep, for example with a quick message before any purchase over 100 units.

You both agree on the core facts. A spent 120 units of shared money without the discussion you'd agreed on for purchases over 100. A, you've acknowledged that, and your belief that the item helps you both can be true at the same time. B, feeling left out of a shared decision makes sense. Still, 'always' and 'impulsive' describe A as a person instead of this one event, and that can make it harder to talk. You might each say what the agreement protects for you. Then decide together what happens next time something feels urgent or obviously useful, such as a quick text before buying.

You both describe real hurt. B felt left out, and A felt upset at being questioned. The facts are clear on one point: the purchase went above the 100-unit limit you agreed on, and it wasn't discussed first. A, you acknowledge knowing that. It may help to look at this one purchase on its own rather than calling it 'always,' since one example doesn't show a pattern. You could talk about why the agreement matters to each of you. You might also decide whether you need a quick way to check in for purchases that feel urgent or clearly shared, so neither of you feels sidelined or put on trial.

It makes sense that you felt let down. You put something into that note and heard nothing back, and silence is easy to read as avoidance. From what's described here, though, the note never reached B. A fan blew it behind a cabinet before B came into the room, so B didn't see it that evening. The quiet wasn't a reply at all. You might find the note, or simply tell B what it said, and give B a fair chance to respond to what you meant to share.

It makes sense that you felt confused. A fan blew the note behind the cabinet before you came into the room, so you never had a chance to see it. You didn't ignore anything. It may help to tell A that calmly, and maybe look behind the cabinet together so the note turns up. Since you only learned about it after A got upset, you could also ask what the note said and why it mattered so much. A likely felt let down by what seemed like no response, while you had no idea there was anything to respond to.

It sounds like a fan moved the note behind the cabinet before B came in, so B never saw it. A, your hurt makes sense. You reached out, heard nothing back, and that felt like being avoided. B, your confusion makes sense too, because you were reacting to a note you didn't know existed. Nobody ignored anyone here. The message just never arrived. It might help to talk through what the note said now. Next time, a quick text or a word in person could back up anything important you leave in writing.

It sounds like a fan caused this misunderstanding, not either of you. A, it makes sense that you felt let down when your note got no reply. But B never saw it, because it blew behind the cabinet before B came in, so the silence wasn't B avoiding you. B, your confusion makes sense too, since you didn't know there was a note at all. It might help to find the note together and talk about what it said. Next time something matters, a quick text or a word in person can back up the note.

Thank you for describing what happened. You clearly said you wanted to leave, and your partner stood in the only doorway for five minutes so you couldn't. Feeling afraid in that situation makes sense. Wanting space during an argument is reasonable. Being physically kept from leaving, even briefly, is a serious matter and is widely seen as a warning sign in relationships. It may help to talk with someone you trust, a counselor, or a domestic-abuse helpline about what happened and how to stay safe. If you ever feel in immediate danger, please contact emergency services.

B, it sounds like it felt really distressing to have the argument stop before it was settled, and that feeling makes sense. But standing in the only doorway after A asked to leave meant A couldn't leave for five minutes. However urgent things feel, physically keeping a partner in a room isn't okay. It takes away their choice and can feel frightening or controlling, even if you didn't mean it that way. Next time, try agreeing on a pause and a set time to come back to the conversation. Calming yourself during that gap may help both of you. If this panic keeps coming up, a counselor could help you work with it safely.

B, your panic about leaving things unfinished is real. But standing in the only doorway after A asked to leave kept A in the room against their will for five minutes. That is a safety issue, not just a disagreement about how to communicate. A, feeling afraid when you couldn't leave makes sense. A conversation can't be resolved by keeping someone from leaving. Going forward, you could agree that either of you can take a break at any time, with a set time to come back to the talk. If blocking exits or fear keeps happening, please consider getting support. Hotlines and counselors can help you both stay safe.

B, your panic about leaving things unfinished is real and worth taking seriously. But standing in the only doorway after A asked to leave kept A in the room against their will for five minutes. That isn't a way to reach a resolution, and A was frightened by it. A, wanting space and being afraid are both understandable, and you have the right to leave a conversation. A better approach could be to agree on a pause and a set time to come back to the topic. If blocking or fear happens again, it would be wise to talk to a counselor or a domestic-violence support line.
